locations.quote: **A university research chair, or a team of similar size, operates shared infra‑structure: Linux hosts with graphics processors reached over Secure Shell (SSH), a Slack workspace, a GitHub organisation, and a handful of internal dashboards and databases. Its people change every semester, because thesis students, external collaborators, and working students join and leave on their own dates. Whoever needs access to any part of this infrastructure asks for it by chat message or e‑mail.**

generated.title: Paragraph exceeds recommended length
generated.description: Paragraph in Section 1.2 Existing Infrastructure spans more than 10 lines, reducing readability.

locations.quote: **Keycloak serves as the identity provider of the chair. It handles OpenID Connect (OIDC) login, groups, and profle attributes such as SSH public keys, and its Fine‑Grained Admin Permissions restrict an administrative right to a single group [Key26]. The Linux hosts read this directory over the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) through nslcd, sshd, pam_access, and sudoers, and an Ansible role confgures each host. Slack and GitHub manage membership through their own application programming interfaces (APIs) 1 and tokens, and neither shares an administrative interface with Keycloak.**

generated.title: Paragraph exceeds recommended length
generated.description: Paragraph in Section 2 Problem spans more than 10 lines, reducing readability.

locations.quote: **Requesters do not know who manages which resource. A student who needs a host, a channel, and a repository asks several people and meanwhile borrows the session of a colleague or works under a shared account. Bauer et al. observed this workaround in far more mature organisations [Bau+09], and Beautement et al. 1https://api.slack.com/ and https://docs.github.com/en/rest 2.**

generated.title: Paragraph exceeds recommended length
generated.description: Paragraph in Section 3 Motivation spans more than 10 lines, reducing readability.

locations.quote: **Access that ends on its own changes the question an organisation answers: it no longer asks who still needs a grant, but only who wants more time. The requester describes a need once, in terms of a project, and receives working access within minutes. The maintainer keeps the judgement over a request without holding any privilege in the identity provider, and the super admin works through a queue of vetted requests instead of interruptions. The auditor receives evidence as a by‑product of normal operation. Research on access control supplies the building blocks for this vision. Role‑based access control gave organisations a shared vocabulary for who may do what [San+96], and Ferraiolo et al. consolidated its models into a reference standard [Fer+01]. Bertino et al. attach enabling and disabling events to roles in their temporal model. [BBF01] Joshi et al. generalise this idea to role assignments with a limited duration [Jos+05].**
